# Adam Smith and the Concept of “the Economy”

YAN CHE In this paper, I argue that Adam Smith develops an account of “the economy” in his 1776 Wealth of Nations that both mimetically represents precise units of economic activity and invokes a sense of the sublime incomprehensibility of the total economy. Drawing on Smith’s The History of Astronomy and his engagement with Newtonianism, I show that this apparent contradiction arises from Smith’s argument for the necessity of fancy and wonder in forming intellectual systems. The contrast between a sublime totality and individually delineated parts is a feature of a persistent strain of eighteenth-century thought, and Smith recreates this tension when he conceives of the workings of the economy in physiological terms. Likewise, Smith’s reliance on the motif of “multiplication by division” connects economic with intellectual production as phenomena whose processes of explication require acts of imagination to bridge the limits of the understanding. The conceptual gap I highlight between the workings of the parts and the whole casts new light on Smith’s approach to political economy. In particular, I show that Smith’s famous “invisible hand” is not a straightforward metaphor for the “natural” operations of the economy. Rather, I argue that Smith is concerned with describing how individual motivations and incentives aggregate into larger economic outcomes through a similar mechanism of “multiplication by division.”
